(a) the Sparse Incomparabilty Lemma holds for every graph H (and, more precisely, for every graph H' with atmost k vertices there exists an H' uniquely H-colorable graph G with girt at least k), (b) there exists a 1-1 correspondance between the set of H-colorings of a graph G and the set of H' uniquely H'-colorable graphs H' with girth at most l, (c) the above correspondence
the existence of a homomorphism between two graphs can be decided by the existence of a subgraph of a third graph, and that for every graph there exist sparse uniquely H-colorizable graphs.

In summary, our research is concerned with

the following questions: What can be said about the existence of homomorphisms from H to G? What can be said if G is sparse and H is not? What can be deduced from the existence of homorphisms G → G' and H → H' for all G' and H' with atmost k vertices?

the existence of sparse graphs with given homomorphisms or colorings.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
for every graph there exists a sparse graph with the same colorings and homomorphic properties as the original graph.
the existence of sparse graphs with given H-colorings (and homomorphisms) is determined by H and the number of colors k, and is independent of the number l of vertices.
the existence of a homomorphism from a graph G to a graph H can be characterized by a certain combinatorial property of the graph H, which depends only on H and is independent of the graph G.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the theory of sparse graphs with given homomorphisms is essentially the same as that of dense graphs with given colorations.
we provide a unified approach to a wide range of results concerning sparse graphs and graph homomorphisms.
the existence of sparse graphs with given homomorphisms to a fixed graph H is equivalent to the existence of sparse homomorphisms from H to H.
The main takeaway from our work is that
in the case of graphs with given colorability and homomorphability properties the sparse graphs are as rich and versatile as their dense counterparts.
the study of sparse graphs with given homomorphisms or colorings may provide a useful alternative to the study of sparse uniquely k-colorable graphs.
in many situations one can replace the homomorphisms between graphs with the homomorphims between their colorings, which are easier to work with.
